domain: Monetary Economics / Financial Infrastructure / Technology Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the emergence of electronic/digital money from the 1960s through 2000s, examining the structural gap between when digital money 'became thinkable' (conceptual frameworks, regulatory recognition) versus when it was 'first held' (operational infrastructure, consumer adoption). The topic tests whether this temporal gap constitutes a contested kernel with different readings of what counts as 'emergence,' or whether it collapses into a single constraint about institutional lag.

key_entities: European Monetary Institute / ECB (regulatory authority, EMD 2000)
Federal Reserve (monetary aggregate authority, discontinued M3 reporting)
Commercial banks (infrastructure operators and regulatory subjects)
key_tensions: Infrastructure operational (SWIFT 1977, ACH 1972) vs regulatory framework (EMD 2000) — 23-28 year lag
Interbank settlement systems vs consumer-facing 'holding' of digital money
M4/M5 monetary aggregates discontinued as inadequate to capture digital money reality
Market innovation (credit cards 1950s, PayPal 1998) vs regulatory standardization (EMD 2000)
key_mechanisms: SWIFT messaging protocol (interbank communication without direct consumer access)
ACH batch processing (enables direct deposit, bill payment without consumer 'holding')
Magnetic stripe cards (consumer possession of digital access token, not digital money itself)
key_absences: No clear definition of when 'digital money' as distinct from 'electronic payment infrastructure' emerged
Absence of consumer deposit insurance frameworks for digital money until EMD 2000
No discussion of central bank digital currency (CBDC) as alternative reading of 'digital money'

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The temporal boundary of when 'digital money' emerged — whether emergence is defined by infrastructure operationality, regulatory recognition, consumer adoption, or conceptual thinkability
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Contested between technological determinists (infrastructure = emergence), legal positivists (regulatory framework = emergence), and monetary theorists (M-aggregate capture = emergence)
commitment_system_recognition.collapse_reason: The supposed readings do not emit structurally different constraints. All readings agree that digital money emerged through a multi-decade process with infrastructure preceding regulation. The disagreement is about which milestone to privilege in a narrative timeline, not about what constraints digital money imposes. Infrastructure-first and regulation-first readings would both identify the same beneficiaries (banks, payment processors), the same victims (unbanked populations, privacy advocates), and the same extractiveness profile (transaction fees, data harvesting). This is one constraint read from different observer positions (technological vs legal vs monetary), not multiple constraints from one kernel.

axes.selection_reason: Highest centrality; captures the core 'became thinkable vs first held' tension as institutional lag rather than contested kernel

axes.primary_observable: Federal Reserve discontinuation of M3 reporting; ECB treatment of e-money in M-aggregates
axes.selection_reason: Mountain providing measurement constraint; structurally distinct from institutional lag axis

axes.selection_reason: Snare with distinct victim set; captures exclusion dimension absent from other axes

omegas.description: The 'became thinkable vs first held' framing does not constitute a contested kernel. Infrastructure-first and regulation-first readings emit the same constraint (institutional lag benefiting incumbents) with the same beneficiary/victim structure. The disagreement is about narrative emphasis, not structural difference.

Is monetary_aggregate_collapse a true Mountain (measurement impossibility) or a Piton (central bank policy choice to discontinue reporting)? If central banks could have adapted M-aggregates but chose not to, the constraint type changes.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + F03 (Hasty Generalization)

omegas.description: If central banks had issued digital currency in the 1970s-1990s, would infrastructure_regulatory_lag have occurred? The absence of CBDC may be the upstream cause of the lag, not a separate axis.
omegas.source: Deferred axis cbdc_absence + Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan)

omegas.description: Privacy-surveillance drift may be the highest-epsilon snare in the system, but was deferred due to centrality scoring. If transaction surveillance is the primary extractive mechanism, the selection may have missed the core constraint.
